Mr. Shah Hossain also submits that the plaintiff-petitioners produced and exhibited the certified copy of their title deed in support of their claim to the suit land without any formal proof thereof and as such those secondary evidence in support of their title is not admissible in law within the meaning of Section 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act, 1872. To substantiate his submission, Mr. Hossain cited the decisions reported in 47 DLR (AD) 45; 41 DLR (AD) 97 and 14 BLC (AD) 132.  27. Mr. Shah Hossain finally submits that the trial Court wrongly shifted the burden of proving the correctness of S. A. Khatian on the defendant-opposite parties and held that the defendants failed to proves as to how, why and when the suit land became the khas land of the Government by adducing any evidence, oral and documentary. On this point Mr. Hossain further submits that as plaintiff-the petitioners ought to have proved their case, they cannot take the advantage of the weakness of the defendants. Supporting the impugned judgment and decree Mr. Hossain lastly submits that the appellate court below as the final court of fact arrived at a proper decision upon proper assessment of the pleadings of the parties, evidence and other materials on record and as such the same does not call for any interference from this Court. 

 34. It is a settled principle of law that the plaintiff has to proves his case on the balance of probabilities and he/she cannot bank or capitalize on the weakness of the defendant. It is also a settled proposition that burden of proof shifts and the question of onus loses importance when both the sides adduce evidence in support of their claim and defence. In the case of Muhammad Ishaque vs Ekramul Haque Chowdhury and others II ADC 50 our apex Court held that ".... It is well-settled that when both the parties have led evidence question of onus is out of place and the matter is to be decided on the evidence led by the parties. " 

 40. As I have already found that the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 are mere trespassers into the suit land, they have got no locus standi to question the accuracy or genuineness of the title deed of the plaintiff petitioners however defective title the latter might have to the suit land. On the 'balance of probabilities' which is the standard of proof in civil jurisdiction as opposed to 'beyond reasonable double' in criminal jurisdiction and also on the weight of evidence and preponderance of documents available in the records of the suit, it appears to me that the plaintiff-petitioners have lawful title to the suit land, which can be questioned only by a person having a better title thereto. That being so, the suit of the plaintiffs succeeds and the defendants having failed to prove their better title to the suit land than that of the plaintiffs, they are entitled to a decree as prayed for.
